title: The Spec and the Cost Sheet
bigQuestion: How do you turn a big idea into a plan that someone else could pick up and follow?

story.title: Twelve Chairs, Three Courses, One Notebook
story.kicker: A senior offers to cook a real dinner for twelve and discovers that the cooking is the easy part.
paragraphs: Marisol had cooked for her family for years, so when her grandmother's seventieth birthday came around, she said the words before she thought them through: "I'll make the dinner. Three courses. Twelve people." Her aunt raised an eyebrow and asked one question. "What are you serving?" Marisol realized she had no idea.

That night she opened a notebook and wrote the date at the top. Then she stared at the blank page. A soup, maybe. Chicken, because her grandmother liked it. Something sweet. But how much chicken feeds twelve? How many pots did she own? When did the soup need to start if dinner was at six? She did not know a single number yet.

Her FCS teacher had a phrase for this moment. "A wish is not a plan. A plan has numbers, tools and a clock." Marisol started with the guests. Twelve people, one with a shellfish allergy, two who did not eat pork, one small cousin who ate almost nothing. That list changed the menu before she had bought a thing.

By the end of the week the notebook had a menu with quantities, a cost sheet with every item and its price, a list of every pot and pan, and a timeline that started two days before the party. It also had a page called Safety with the food thermometer temperatures written in ink. The dinner was still ten days away, and Marisol already felt like she had done half the work.

She had. In this chapter you will do the same for a project of your own, a meal for a group or a piece of clothing you sew. You will write a specification, cost every part, plan every hour and decide ahead of time what a good result will look like.
story.think: What is one question Marisol should have asked before she offered to cook, and what number would answering it give her?

lessons.title: Pick a Project You Can Finish
lessons.mainIdea: A good capstone project is one you can plan, afford, complete on time and evaluate against a clear standard.
reading: Picture two students on the first day of the capstone. One wants to sew a lined wool coat with a zipper and welt pockets. The other wants to make a hemmed apron with two patch pockets. Both are real sewing projects, but only one can be finished in six class periods by a student who has made one drawstring bag. The first step of any project is choosing something that fits the time, the budget, the tools and your own skill.

Use four questions to test an idea. Can I finish it in the time I have? Can I pay for it with the budget I have? Do I have, or can I borrow, every tool it needs? Have I already done the hardest step at least once? If the answer to any question is no, shrink the idea until every answer is yes. A three-course dinner for twelve becomes a two-course dinner for eight. A coat becomes a vest.

Shrinking is not failing. A finished apron with straight seams and even pockets shows more skill than a half-done coat. Employers, judges and teachers all grade the result you deliver, not the one you imagined. Write your idea in one sentence, such as "I will cook a soup, a main dish and a dessert for twelve guests on May 9" or "I will sew a lined tote bag from a commercial pattern by May 9." Every later page of the plan grows from that sentence.

words.d: a final project that pulls together the skills learned across a whole course
the size of a project: what it includes and what it leaves out
a limit you must work within, such as time, money, tools or skill

look.title: Four Ideas, One Choice
look.text: A student has six 50-minute class periods, $30 (example) and access to the school kitchen. Four ideas: (A) a wedding cake with three tiers and fondant; (B) a pan of lasagna and a green salad for ten; (C) a seven-course tasting menu; (D) a batch of handmade croissants, which take two days of folding and chilling.
look.prompt: Which idea passes all four questions, and which single constraint knocks out each of the others?

check.q: A student wants to sew a lined wool coat but has only made one drawstring bag. Which question about the project does this most clearly fail?
choices: Have I done the hardest step before?
Can I afford the fabric?
Is there a sewing machine available?
Is there enough time?
check.why: Skill is one of the four tests. A coat's lining, zipper and welt pockets are all steps this student has never done.

check.q: What is the best response when a project idea fails one of the four questions?
choices: Keep the idea and hope for extra time
Shrink the idea until every answer is yes
Ask a friend to do the hard steps
Drop the capstone and do a written report
check.why: Shrinking the scope keeps the project real and finishable. A smaller finished project shows more skill than a large unfinished one.

check.q: Which sentence is a usable one-line project statement?
choices: I want to make something nice for my family
I will cook a great meal sometime this spring
I will sew a lined tote bag from a commercial pattern by May 9
I will learn to cook
check.why: A project statement names the product, the method and the date. The others leave out the what, the how or the when.

lessons.title: Writing a Specification
lessons.mainIdea: A specification describes the finished product in measurable terms so anyone can tell whether the result meets it.
reading: Imagine handing your plan to a friend who has never seen your project and asking them to make it while you are away. Every question they would have to ask you is a hole in your *specification*. A specification, or spec, is a written description of the finished product: what it is, who it is for, how big it is, what it must do and what it must not contain. Engineers, chefs, tailors and builders all write one before they start.

For a meal, the spec lists the number of guests, the courses, the dishes in each course, the portion size per person, the serving time, and any dietary limits. Example: "Serves 12. Course 1: tomato soup, 1 cup each. Course 2: roast chicken, 6 oz each, with rice and green beans. Course 3: lemon bars, 2 per person. Served at 6:00 p.m. No shellfish. No pork. One child portion at half size." Every line can be checked with a measuring cup, a scale or a clock.

For a sewn piece, the spec names the pattern number and view, the size, the fabric type and yardage, the color, the notions such as thread, zipper and interfacing, the finished measurements, and the seam finish. Example: "Tote bag, pattern view B, 14 by 16 inches finished, medium-weight cotton canvas, lined, 5/8-inch seams pressed open, straps 24 inches long, all seams zigzag finished."

Write in *measurable* terms. "Enough chicken" is not measurable; "6 oz per person, 4.5 lb total" is. "A nice color" is not measurable; "navy blue canvas" is. When you evaluate the project at the end, you will hold the result against this spec line by line, so every line must be something you can see, weigh, measure or time.

words.d: a written, measurable description of what the finished product must be
able to be checked with a tool such as a scale, a ruler, a thermometer or a clock
the amount of one food served to one person
the small sewing supplies a pattern calls for: thread, zippers, buttons, interfacing, elastic

look.title: Find the Holes
look.text: A draft spec reads: "Dinner for my family. Some kind of pasta with sauce, a salad, and dessert. Serve around dinnertime. Make plenty. Watch out for Uncle Ray's allergy." A friend has to cook this without you.
look.prompt: List every question the friend would have to ask, then rewrite the spec so each question is already answered with a number or a name.

check.q: Which line belongs in a specification because it is measurable?
choices: Roast chicken, 6 oz per person, 12 servings
A generous amount of chicken
Chicken cooked the way Grandma likes it
Plenty of chicken for everyone
check.why: A spec line must be checkable with a tool. Ounces and servings can be weighed and counted; the others cannot.

check.q: A sewing spec should include the fabric yardage. Why?
choices: So the project looks professional
So the teacher knows you read the pattern
Because it fixes the largest cost and tells you exactly what to buy
Because yardage decides the seam allowance
check.why: Fabric is usually the biggest cost in a sewn project, and the yardage on the pattern envelope tells you the exact amount to purchase.

check.q: A spec says "No shellfish" and "One child portion at half size." What kind of information is this?
choices: Decoration
Cost
Timeline
Dietary limits and portion rules for specific guests
check.why: The spec records who the meal is for, including allergies, food rules and special portions, so the plan protects each guest.

lessons.title: Know Your Audience
lessons.mainIdea: The people you serve or sew for shape the spec: their number, ages, allergies, food rules, sizes and tastes come before your own preferences.
reading: Marisol's guest list changed her menu before she bought a single ingredient. A shellfish *allergy* meant no shrimp. Two guests who did not eat pork meant chicken, not ham. A small cousin meant a mild dish and a half portion. Your project exists for other people, so the second page of your plan is a plain list of who they are and what they need.

For a meal, gather: the exact head count, any allergies (the nine major allergens are milk, eggs, fish, shellfish, tree nuts, peanuts, wheat, soybeans and sesame), religious or personal food rules, ages, and anything the host tells you about likes and dislikes. Ask directly and write the answers down. An allergy is a safety matter, not a preference, so an allergen must be kept out of the dish and off the shared cutting board, not just left off the plate.

For a sewn garment, gather the wearer's body measurements taken with a tape over light clothing: bust or chest, waist, hips, back length and any other line the pattern envelope asks for. Compare them to the pattern's size chart and choose the size by the measurements, not by the store size the person usually wears. Ask about fabric feel, color and how the piece will be washed. A shirt for someone who will machine wash it hot should not be cut from a dry-clean-only fabric.

Respect what people tell you. A family that eats no meat on certain days, a guest who fasts, a wearer who wants long sleeves for religious reasons: these are not obstacles to work around but the requirements the spec is built on. The best cooks and tailors are the ones who listen first.

words.d: a food that causes a dangerous immune reaction in some people; nine are named on U.S. labels
the exact number of people who will be served
the table on a pattern envelope that matches body measurements to pattern sizes

look.title: Guest List for the Birthday Dinner (example)
look.prompt: Using these rows, which ingredients must stay out of the whole menu, and how would you size the portions for the child?

check.q: One guest has a peanut allergy. Which plan protects that guest?
choices: Serve the peanut dish but tell the guest which one it is
Leave peanuts out of every dish and keep peanut products off shared boards and utensils
Put the peanuts on the side so they can be skipped
Serve peanuts only in the dessert
check.why: An allergen is a safety hazard. Trace amounts from a shared board or spoon can cause a reaction, so it must be kept out of the kitchen for that meal.

check.q: How should you choose a pattern size for someone you are sewing for?
choices: Use the size they buy in stores
Guess from how they look
Measure their body and compare to the pattern's size chart
Pick the middle size on the envelope
check.why: Pattern sizes do not match store sizes. The envelope's size chart is keyed to real body measurements.

check.q: A host tells you two guests eat no meat on Fridays and the dinner is on a Friday. What is this information for your plan?
choices: A preference you can ignore if the menu is set
A reason to move the dinner
Something to mention at the table
A requirement the spec must be built around
check.why: Food rules from faith or personal choice are requirements of the project, recorded in the spec and honored in the menu.

lessons.title: Every Ingredient, Every Material
lessons.mainIdea: A cost sheet lists every single item the project uses, with its unit price and the amount needed, so the total is real and not a guess.
reading: Look at Marisol's first cost estimate: "Chicken, rice, beans, soup stuff, dessert stuff: about $60." Now look at her second: twenty-three lines, each with an item, a package size, a package price, the amount she actually needs and the cost of that amount. The first number was a wish. The second was a *cost sheet*. The difference was two hours in a grocery store aisle with her phone and a notebook.

Build the sheet from the recipes, not from memory. Open each recipe, scaled to your head count, and copy every ingredient down, including the ones that seem too small to matter: salt, oil, the parchment paper, the foil. For a sewing project, copy every line from the pattern envelope's back: fabric, lining, interfacing, thread, zipper, buttons, and add the things the envelope does not list, such as a new machine needle or a marking pen.

Give the sheet five columns: item, package size and price, unit price, amount needed, and cost of the amount needed. Unit price is the package price divided by the package size. Example: a 5-lb bag of rice at $4.50 (example) is $0.90 per lb. If the recipe needs 3 lb, the cost line is 3 × $0.90 = $2.70. Do this for every line, then add the column. That sum is your ingredient or material cost.

Forgetting a line is the most common mistake, and the forgotten line is usually a cheap one that turns into a trip to the store on the day of the event. The second most common mistake is copying the package price into the cost column when you only use part of the package. You will still have to buy the whole package, so keep a sixth column for what you will actually spend at the register.

words.d: a table listing every item a project uses, its unit price, the amount needed and the resulting cost
the price of one unit of an item, found by dividing the package price by the package size
one row on a cost sheet: a single ingredient or material

look.title: Unit Prices From the Store Shelf (example)
look.cite: example prices for practice; real prices vary by store and season
look.prompt: The chicken course needs 4.5 lb of thighs, 3 lb of rice and 3 lb of green beans. Compute each cost line and the total for the course.

check.q: A 5-lb bag of rice costs $4.50 (example). The recipe needs 3 lb. What goes in the cost column?
check.why: Unit price is $4.50 ÷ 5 = $0.90 per lb, and 3 lb × $0.90 = $2.70.

check.q: Where should the list of ingredients on a cost sheet come from?
choices: Memory of what is usually in the dish
The scaled recipe, line by line
The store's weekly ad
A friend's shopping list
check.why: Copying from the scaled recipe catches every ingredient, including small ones like salt, oil and parchment that memory skips.

check.q: Why keep a separate column for the register total when a recipe uses only part of a package?
choices: Because you still have to buy the whole package
Because sales tax is added later
Because the unit price is only an estimate
Because leftovers must be thrown out
check.why: The cost column shows what the project consumes; the register column shows the cash you must have, since stores sell whole packages.

lessons.title: Scaling Recipes to the Head Count
lessons.mainIdea: To scale a recipe, divide the servings you need by the servings it makes to get a factor, then multiply every ingredient by that factor and convert to sensible units.
reading: Marisol's lemon bar recipe makes 12 bars in an 8-by-8-inch pan. Her spec says 2 bars each for 12 people, which is 24 bars. The *scaling factor* is 24 ÷ 12 = 2. Every ingredient is multiplied by 2: 1 cup of flour becomes 2 cups, ½ cup of butter becomes 1 cup, 3 eggs become 6, 2 Tbsp of lemon juice become 4 Tbsp, which is ¼ cup. Two 8-by-8 pans, or one 9-by-13, hold the doubled batch.

Factors are not always whole numbers. A soup recipe that serves 8 must serve 12, so the factor is 12 ÷ 8 = 1.5. If the soup calls for 4 cups of broth, the scaled amount is 6 cups, which is 1.5 quarts. If it calls for 1 Tbsp of oil, you need 1.5 Tbsp, which is 1 Tbsp plus 1.5 tsp, since 3 tsp make 1 Tbsp. Write the scaled amount in the unit you can actually measure.

Some things do not scale in a straight line. Cooking time rises for a larger pot but not by the factor; a doubled roast does not take twice as long, so you cook by internal temperature and a thermometer, never by the clock alone. Seasonings like salt and hot pepper are usually scaled by the factor and then tasted and adjusted. Pan size must be checked separately, because a doubled cake batter in the original pan overflows.

Compute every scaled line twice, once when you write it and once the next day, and mark the sheet with the check. A single arithmetic slip, such as writing 2 tsp when you meant 2 Tbsp, is a small mistake on paper and a ruined dish in the pan, and it is the kind of error a second look always catches.

words.d: the number you multiply each ingredient by: servings needed divided by servings the recipe makes
how much a recipe makes, in servings or pieces
the temperature at the center of a food, read with a food thermometer

look.title: Scale the Soup
look.text: Tomato soup, serves 8: 2 Tbsp olive oil, 1 onion, 2 cans (28 oz each) crushed tomatoes, 4 cups broth, 1 tsp salt, ½ cup cream. The spec needs 12 servings of 1 cup each.
look.prompt: Find the factor, rewrite every line in a unit you can measure, and state which line you would taste and adjust rather than trust the math.

check.q: A recipe serves 8 and you need 12 servings. What is the scaling factor?
check.why: Servings needed ÷ servings the recipe makes = 12 ÷ 8 = 1.5.

check.q: A recipe calls for 2 Tbsp lemon juice and the factor is 2. Which is the scaled amount written in a measurable unit?
choices: ¼ cup
4 tsp
½ cup
2 Tbsp
check.why: 2 Tbsp × 2 = 4 Tbsp, and 4 Tbsp = ¼ cup.

check.q: You double a chicken recipe. How should you decide when the chicken is done?
choices: Double the cooking time
Read 165 °F at the thickest part with a food thermometer
Use the original time
Cook until the outside is brown
check.why: Cooking time does not scale by the factor. Poultry is done at a safe minimum internal temperature of 165 °F, checked with a thermometer.

lessons.title: Hidden Costs and the Budget Line
lessons.mainIdea: Beyond ingredients or fabric, a real cost sheet includes supplies, equipment you must buy or rent, a waste allowance and a cushion, compared against the budget you were given.
reading: A student sewing a tote bag priced the canvas, lining, thread and webbing and came to $18.40 (example). Then the machine needle broke on the first seam, the interfacing was not on the sheet, and the bag needed a magnetic snap the pattern had listed in tiny print. The real total was $27.10. Nothing on the second list was expensive, but together they were almost half again the first number. These are *hidden costs*, and the cost sheet needs a section for them.

Add a block below the ingredient or material lines. For a meal: foil, parchment, storage containers for leftovers, dish soap, disposable plates or napkins if used, ice, and any equipment you must buy, rent or borrow such as a large stockpot or a second roasting pan. For a sewn piece: needles, marking tools, interfacing, fusible tape, pattern cost, and a pressing cloth. Price each one the same way, unit price times amount.

Then add two lines that are not things at all. The first is a waste allowance, because peeling, trimming and cutting on grain all lose material. Cooks often buy about 10 percent more produce than the recipe weight; sewers buy the envelope's yardage, which already includes layout waste, but add fabric for a matched print or a cutting mistake. The second is a cushion, a small amount, often 5 to 10 percent of the total, held back for a price that rose or an item you forgot.

Finally, write the *budget* line: the money you actually have. Compare the total to it. If the total is higher, change the plan now, not at the register. Swap a store brand for a name brand, choose chicken thighs over breasts, replace fresh berries with frozen, drop the lining or pick a less costly fabric. The spec may change slightly; the budget does not.

words.d: a small necessary expense that is easy to forget, such as foil, needles or interfacing
extra material bought because trimming, peeling and cutting lose some of it
money held back in a budget for a price change or a forgotten item
the amount of money you have to spend on the whole project

look.title: Tote Bag Cost Sheet, Two Versions (example)
look.prompt: Confirm the real total by adding the four hidden lines to the first estimate, then say what a 10 percent cushion on the real total would be.

check.q: A meal's ingredient total is $80 (example). What would a 10 percent cushion be?
check.why: 10 percent of $80 is $8, held back for a price rise or a forgotten item.

check.q: Which item is a hidden cost most students forget on a sewing cost sheet?
choices: The main fabric
The pattern's yardage
The color of the thread
Interfacing listed in small print on the envelope
check.why: Interfacing, needles and snaps are small, necessary and easy to overlook. The main fabric is never forgotten.

check.q: The cost total comes to $95 and the budget is $80 (example). What is the right move?
choices: Buy everything and hope for a sale
Change the plan now, such as store brands or a cheaper cut, until the total fits
Skip the cushion and the waste allowance
Borrow the difference
check.why: The budget is the fixed constraint. The plan is adjusted before shopping, not at the register.

lessons.title: Working Backwards From the Deadline
lessons.mainIdea: Build the timeline from the finish time backwards, giving each task its real duration, so that the longest and earliest jobs start first.
reading: Dinner is at 6:00 p.m. A roast chicken takes about 1 hour 30 minutes in the oven plus 15 minutes of rest, so it goes in at 4:15. The oven must preheat, so it is turned on at 4:00. The chicken must be seasoned before that, at 3:45. Read those times again: they were found by starting at the end and stepping backwards. That is how every timeline for a project is built.

List every task the project needs, including the ones that are not cooking or sewing: shopping, washing produce, thawing, preheating, pressing fabric, cutting, resting, cooling, plating, cleanup. Next to each, write how long it really takes, timed from experience or from the recipe or pattern, not from hope. Then place the last task at the deadline and work backwards, task by task, until you reach the first thing you must do.

Thawing is the task most often placed wrong. A 4-to-5-lb chicken thaws in the refrigerator in about a day, so it moves from freezer to fridge two days before the dinner to be safe. It never thaws on the counter, because the outside sits in the danger zone of 40 to 140 °F while the inside is still frozen. Dessert that must cool and set, such as lemon bars, is baked the day before. Fabric is washed, dried and pressed the day before cutting.

Mark *checkpoints*: a few moments where you stop and confirm that you are on schedule. "Day before, 8 p.m.: dessert baked and chilled, chicken thawed, all produce washed. Day of, 3:30: soup simmering, oven on at 4:00." A missed checkpoint tells you early enough to fix it, by simplifying a dish or asking for help, instead of at 5:55 with twelve people at the table.

words.d: a schedule that lists every task with its start time, built backwards from the deadline
a set moment in the timeline where you confirm the work is on schedule
40 to 140 °F, the temperature range where bacteria in food multiply fastest

look.title: Put the Evening in Order
look.text: Dinner at 6:00. Tasks with real durations: rest the chicken 15 min; roast 90 min; preheat oven 15 min; season chicken 10 min; cook rice 25 min; steam green beans 8 min; reheat soup 15 min; set the table 10 min. Only one person is cooking.
look.prompt: Write the start time for each task working backwards from 6:00, and name which tasks can overlap while the chicken roasts.

check.q: A chicken needs 90 minutes to roast and 15 minutes to rest, and dinner is at 6:00. When does it go in the oven?
check.why: Work backwards: 6:00 minus 15 minutes rest is 5:45, minus 90 minutes roasting is 4:15.

check.q: Why must a frozen chicken be moved to the refrigerator two days before the dinner?
choices: So it can marinate
Because the freezer must be emptied
Because a large bird takes about a day to thaw in the fridge, and counter thawing leaves it in the danger zone
So it will roast faster
check.why: Refrigerator thawing keeps the whole bird at or below 40 °F. A counter lets the outside sit between 40 and 140 °F for hours.

check.q: What is the purpose of a checkpoint in the timeline?
choices: To mark when guests arrive
To record the cost of each task
To decide the menu
To catch a delay early enough to fix it
check.why: A checkpoint compares the plan to the clock while there is still time to simplify or get help.

lessons.title: The Materials and Equipment List
lessons.mainIdea: List every tool and piece of equipment for every step, check that you have it or can borrow it, and stage it before you start.
reading: Marisol's soup recipe said "blend until smooth." She did not own a blender. She found this out at 3:40 p.m. on the day of the party, with a pot of hot chunky soup in front of her. A tool list would have caught it a week earlier. For each step in the recipe or pattern, write the tool that step needs, then walk through your kitchen or sewing room and check each one off.

Group the list by station. For a meal: prep (cutting boards, one for raw meat and one for produce, a chef's knife, a paring knife, peeler, measuring cups and spoons, bowls), cooking (pots by size, roasting pan, sheet pans, tongs, spatula, whisk, food thermometer), serving (platters, ladle, serving spoons, twelve of every plate, bowl and glass), and storage (containers with lids, foil, labels). For sewing: cutting (shears, rotary cutter and mat, pins, weights), marking (chalk, tracing paper), sewing (machine, correct needle, bobbins, seam ripper), pressing (iron, board, pressing cloth), and finishing (hand needles, tape measure).

Count the ones that matter. Twelve guests need twelve bowls and twelve spoons, plus serving pieces. A three-course dinner may need more pots on the stove than you have burners, which changes the timeline, not just the list. If something is missing, decide now: borrow it, buy it and add it to the cost sheet, or change the method. Soup can be left chunky; a potato masher stands in for a blender.

The day before, stage the equipment: pull it out, wash it, and set it where it will be used. A thermometer that lives in a drawer gets forgotten; one sitting beside the stove gets used. This is *mise en place* for tools, the same idea as measuring ingredients before you cook, and it is the single habit that most separates a calm cook from a frantic one.

words.d: every tool, pan, machine and serving piece a project needs, checked against what you have
one area of a kitchen or workroom set up for one kind of task, such as prep or pressing
French for everything in its place: tools and ingredients ready before work starts
a probe thermometer that reads the internal temperature of food

look.title: Walk the Recipe for Tools
look.text: Recipe steps: (1) dice 2 onions and mince 4 garlic cloves; (2) sauté in a 6-quart pot; (3) add tomatoes and broth, simmer 25 min; (4) blend until smooth; (5) stir in cream, taste; (6) ladle 1 cup into each of 12 bowls. The kitchen has a 4-quart pot, one cutting board, a chef's knife, a wooden spoon and a potato masher.
look.prompt: Name the tool each step needs, mark which ones are missing, and decide for each missing one whether to borrow, buy or change the method.

check.q: Why should raw chicken and salad greens be cut on separate boards?
choices: Greens stain a wooden board
To prevent cross-contamination of ready-to-eat food with raw-meat bacteria
The knife stays sharper
Chicken needs a larger board
check.why: Raw poultry juices carry bacteria that cooking would kill in the chicken but that would survive on uncooked greens.

check.q: A three-course dinner needs five pots at once and the stove has four burners. What does this change?
choices: The head count
The cost sheet only
The timeline, since some dishes must cook earlier and be held or reheated
Nothing, if you stir quickly
check.why: Equipment limits shape the schedule. A dish cooked ahead is reheated to 165 °F when it is time to serve.

check.q: What does it mean to stage equipment?
choices: Buy it new for the event
Store it in the garage
Photograph it for the report
Pull it out, wash it and set it where it will be used before starting
check.why: Staging is mise en place for tools: a thermometer beside the stove gets used, one in a drawer gets forgotten.

lessons.title: The Safety Plan
lessons.mainIdea: A safety plan writes down the standard temperatures, times and rules for the project before the day, so that safety decisions are already made.
reading: At 5:30 on the day of the dinner, with the soup boiling and the guests arriving, nobody remembers whether chicken is 160 or 165 °F. So the number is written on a page taped to the cabinet a week earlier. A *safety plan* is that page: every safety figure and rule the project depends on, decided in a calm moment and posted where the work happens.

For a meal, the page holds the standard figures. Safe minimum internal temperatures: poultry 165 °F; ground meats 160 °F; whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb and veal 145 °F with a 3-minute rest; fish 145 °F; leftovers reheated to 165 °F; eggs cooked until firm. Cold food is held at or below 40 °F and the freezer at 0 °F. The two-hour rule: perishable food that has sat out for more than two hours, or one hour above 90 °F, is discarded. Hands are washed for 20 seconds before starting, after touching raw meat, and after any interruption. Raw meat gets its own board. A lid and baking soda sit near the stove for a grease fire, and water never goes on one.

For a sewing project, the page covers the machine and the iron. Fingers stay clear of the needle; the foot is off the pedal while threading; pins are removed before the needle reaches them, never sewn over. The iron is set to the fabric's setting, rests on its heel, is never left face down, and is unplugged when the session ends. Shears and rotary blades are closed or capped when set down and carried point down. Long hair is tied back around both the machine and the stove.

Add the allergen line from your audience list to the safety page in large letters, with the rule that the allergen does not enter the kitchen during the project. Add the emergency numbers and the location of the first-aid kit and fire extinguisher. Then sign and date the page. When you evaluate the project, this page is one of the things you will be graded on, and it is the one page where "almost right" is not a passing grade.

words.d: a written page of the standard temperatures, times and rules a project depends on, posted where the work happens
perishable food left out more than two hours, or one hour above 90 °F, must be thrown away
the spread of bacteria from one food or surface to another, such as raw chicken juice onto salad

look.title: Safe Minimum Internal Temperatures
rows: beef, pork, lamb, veal whole cuts, plus 3-min rest
look.cite: USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service, safe minimum internal temperature chart
look.prompt: Which of these figures belong on Marisol's posted safety page for a menu of tomato soup, roast chicken and lemon bars, and where in the timeline will each be checked?

check.q: The roast chicken thermometer reads 150 °F at the thickest part of the thigh. What does the safety plan say?
choices: Serve it; the outside is brown
Keep roasting until it reads 165 °F
Rest it 3 minutes and serve
Serve it and reheat leftovers later
check.why: Poultry's safe minimum internal temperature is 165 °F. The 145 °F with rest rule applies to whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb and veal, not chicken.

check.q: The soup was made the day before. How hot must it be when reheated for serving?
choices: Warm enough to steam
check.why: Leftovers are reheated to an internal temperature of 165 °F.

check.q: Which sewing rule belongs on the safety page?
choices: Sew slowly over pins so they do not fall out
Leave the iron face down so it stays hot
Thread the machine with the pedal ready
Remove pins before the needle reaches them and keep the foot off the pedal while threading
check.why: Sewing over pins can break the needle and send a fragment flying; threading with the foot on the pedal risks a stitched finger.

lessons.title: Writing the Rubric First
lessons.mainIdea: A rubric written before the work names what a good result looks like at each level, so the finished project can be judged fairly against the spec.
reading: Ask a friend to taste your soup and they will say "good." Ask them to score it on a *rubric* and they will tell you the salt was right, the texture was slightly grainy and the portion was exactly one cup. A rubric is a table: the rows are the things that matter, and the columns describe what each row looks like at levels such as excellent, good, needs work and not met. Writing it before the project turns the spec into a scoring tool.

Choose the rows from the spec. For a meal, common rows are: served on time, portion size matches the spec, food safety figures met and recorded, taste and seasoning, texture and doneness, appearance and plating, cost within budget, cleanup complete. For a sewn piece: fits the spec's measurements, seams straight and at 5/8 inch, seam finish as specified, pressing, topstitching even, notions attached securely, cost within budget, finished on time.

Describe each level in words that can be checked. For "served on time": excellent means every course within 5 minutes of the plan; good means within 15 minutes; needs work means one course more than 15 minutes late; not met means a course was not served. For "seams": excellent means every seam at 5/8 inch within 1/16 inch and no puckers; good means one seam off by 1/8 inch; and so on. Numbers make the rubric fair to you and to the judge.

Give each row a weight. Safety and the spec's required items weigh most; appearance weighs less. Then, before you begin, score the plan itself: a plan with no thermometer check in the timeline cannot score excellent on safety. Fix the plan, not the rubric. On the day the project is evaluated, you and your teacher will each fill in the same table, and the conversation about where the scores differ is where the real learning happens.

words.d: a scoring table whose rows are the things that matter and whose columns describe each level of quality
one row of a rubric: a single thing the result is judged on
how much one rubric row counts toward the total score

look.title: Fix the Vague Rubric
look.text: A draft rubric row for a tote bag reads: Seams. Excellent: really good seams. Good: pretty good seams. Needs work: seams are a little off. Not met: bad seams. The spec called for 5/8-inch seams, pressed open, zigzag finished.
look.prompt: Rewrite the four levels so each can be checked with a seam gauge and your eyes, then give the row a weight and explain why.

check.q: When should the rubric for a capstone project be written?
choices: Before the work starts, from the spec
After tasting the final dish
During the presentation
Only if the teacher asks
check.why: A rubric written first turns the spec into a scoring tool and shapes the plan; written afterwards, it just describes what happened.

check.q: Which rubric level description is checkable?
choices: Excellent: the soup is delicious
Excellent: every course served within 5 minutes of the planned time
Excellent: the cook tried hard
Excellent: guests seemed happy
check.why: A checkable level uses a number or a tool. Minutes on a clock can be verified; delicious cannot.

check.q: A plan has no thermometer check anywhere on the timeline. What should change?
choices: The rubric, to drop the safety row
The weight of the appearance row
The plan, to add the temperature check at the right time
The head count
check.why: The plan is fixed to meet the rubric, never the reverse. Safety rows carry the most weight and must be met.

review.q: A student has six class periods and $30 (example). Which project fits the constraints?
choices: A three-tier fondant cake
Two-day croissants
A seven-course tasting menu
Lasagna and salad for ten
review.why: Lasagna and salad can be planned, afforded and finished in the time; each of the others fails time, cost or skill.

review.q: Which line is written the way a specification requires?
choices: Tote bag, 14 by 16 inches finished, cotton canvas, 5/8-inch seams
A nice sturdy bag
A bag big enough for books
A bag like the one in the store
review.why: Specs use measurable terms: dimensions, fabric type and seam allowance can all be checked.

review.q: A 5-lb bag of flour costs $3.00 (example). What is the unit price per pound?
review.why: Package price divided by package size: $3.00 ÷ 5 lb = $0.60 per lb.

review.q: A cookie recipe yields 24 cookies and you need 36. What is the scaling factor?
review.why: 36 ÷ 24 = 1.5, and every ingredient is multiplied by 1.5.

review.q: Dinner is at 7:00. A dish takes 40 minutes to bake and 10 minutes to rest. When does it go in the oven?
review.why: 7:00 minus 10 minutes rest is 6:50, minus 40 minutes baking is 6:10.

review.q: A frozen turkey breast is needed Saturday at 4 p.m. Which thawing plan is safe?
choices: On the counter Saturday morning
In the refrigerator starting Thursday
In a sink of warm water Saturday noon
In the oven on low
review.why: Refrigerator thawing keeps the meat at or below 40 °F the whole time; the counter and warm water leave it in the danger zone.

review.q: Ground beef for the sliders reads 150 °F. What is the safe minimum internal temperature for ground meats?
review.why: Ground meats are safe at 160 °F; 145 °F with a rest applies to whole cuts, and 165 °F to poultry and leftovers.

review.q: What is the purpose of giving a rubric row a weight?
choices: To show how much that criterion counts toward the total, with safety counting most
To make the table look complete
To lower the score of a difficult project
To replace the spec
review.why: Weights rank the criteria. Safety and required spec items carry the most weight; appearance carries less.
